items.title: The four-vertex path has the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Apply the published square-root homogeneous-set bound for $P_4$-free graphs to the singleton forbidden graph $P_4$. That earlier class theorem is already exactly the required graph-level Erdős–Hajnal statement.

items.title: Every graph on at most four vertices has the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Let $H$ have at most four vertices. If $H$ is prime and has four vertices, the published prime-graph theorem forces an induced $P_4$ on all four vertices, so $H=P_4$ and the previous corollary applies; smaller prime graphs are covered by the already-published three-vertex inventory. Otherwise the substitution characterization of prime graphs writes $H$ as a substitution of smaller graphs, and substitution closure finishes the induction.

items.title: The bull graph has the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Unpack the published bull-free class theorem at the single forbidden graph $H=$ bull. Its explicit $|G|^{1/4}$ homogeneous-set bound is stronger than the graph-level Erdős–Hajnal conclusion needed here.

items.title: The prime five-vertex graphs are exactly the bull, $C_5$, $P_5$, and $\overline{P_5}$
items.strategy: Start with a prime five-vertex graph $G$ and use the published prime-graph theorem to find an induced $P_4$ inside it. Let $v$ be the fifth vertex. Up to reversing the path and taking complements, inspect the possible neighbourhoods of $v$ on that $P_4$. The patterns with $0$, $1$, or $4$ neighbours create a nontrivial module; the surviving $2$- and $3$-neighbour patterns are exactly the bull, the five-cycle, the five-vertex path, and its complement.

items.title: Every graph on at most five vertices has the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Let $H$ have at most five vertices. If $H$ is prime, the previous lemma reduces it to the bull, $C_5$, $P_5$, or $\overline{P_5}$, all already handled by earlier pages or their immediate corollaries. If $H$ is not prime, write it as a substitution of smaller graphs and use the four-vertex inventory together with substitution closure.

items.title: The left six-vertex prime $\mathcal H$-graph
The right six-vertex prime $\mathcal H$-graph
The two six-vertex prime $\mathcal H$-graphs have the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: For the left graph, delete two different leaves so that both reduced graphs are the bull. Convert the bull theorem to virality, apply the published two-leaf closure theorem with the same six-vertex graph in both slots, and convert back to the Erdős–Hajnal property. The right graph is defined as the complement of the left one, so complement invariance gives the second conclusion.

items.title: The $E$-graph and co-$E$
The Bird graph and co-Bird
The graphs $H^+$ and $H^-$ for two distinguished vertices
The graphs $H_0,H_1,\ldots,H_5$
The graph $H_0$ has the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: View $H_0$ as the graph obtained by substituting $C_5$ for one endpoint of $K_2$: the other endpoint becomes the wheel hub, adjacent to every cycle vertex. Since $K_2$ is covered by the already-published three-vertex inventory and $C_5$ already has the Erdős–Hajnal property, substitution closure gives the claim.

items.title: The left six-vertex prime $\mathcal H$-graph is prime, and deleting any pendant leaf gives the bull
items.strategy: Write the graph as a triangle with one leaf on each triangle vertex. Deleting a chosen leaf visibly leaves the bull. For primeness, inspect each possible nontrivial candidate module: a leaf is separated from the other two leaves by their support vertices, while any set meeting the triangle and omitting one of its leaves is separated by that leaf.

items.title: The right six-vertex prime $\mathcal H$-graph is the complement of the left one, and is prime
items.strategy: Use the explicit vertex bijection from the right figure to the complement of the left figure and then transport the left graph's module check through complement invariance of modules. This verifies both the source-figure relation and the primeness claim promised in the page title.

items.title: The $E$-graph and co-$E$ by finite adjacency data
items.strategy: List the six vertices so that the $E$-graph is a five-vertex path with a pendant edge at the middle vertex, then take the complement edge-by-edge to obtain co-$E$. The example fixes a concrete labelled model for every later co-$E$ witness.

items.title: The Bird graph and co-Bird by finite adjacency data
items.strategy: Start from the bull and attach one more pendant edge to a horn. The explicit complement then gives co-Bird. Recording the two edge lists now keeps the later Bird and co-Bird structure pages from having to recover them informally from the figure.

items.title: $H_0$ is the five-wheel
items.strategy: Check directly from the edge list that $w$ is adjacent to each vertex of the outer five-cycle and that no other edges are present. This makes the later substitution proof of the Erdős–Hajnal property for $H_0$ completely concrete.

items.title: $H_1$ and $H_5$ arise by the stated labelled leaf attachments
items.strategy: Read the labels on Figure 7 and attach the new leaf $v_i'$ to $v_i$ in order. The example verifies that the recursive description really produces the pictured intermediate graph $H_1$ and the final graph $H_5$.

items.title: Leaf-reducible finite graph families
A sparse graph without a large sparse pair has a large nearly covered sparse pair
items.strategy: Repeat Claim 5.2.1 from the $P_5$ paper and note that its proof uses only the degree bound, the failure of the $2y^4$-sparser outcome, and the failure of the large sparse-pair outcome. The $\overline{P_5}$-free hypothesis is present in the source context but is not touched in the argument.

items.title: Leaf-reducible families yield a large anticomplete pair or a deeper restricted induced subgraph
items.strategy: Choose the leaf-reducible witness $H\in\mathcal F$ with leaf $v$, and let the reduced family be the one from the definition. Convert the reduced family's Erdős–Hajnal property into virality, set the source exponent parameter to $a=bd+2$, and apply Lemma 5.1 of the leaf-extension paper when $y$ is below its threshold. The many-copy outcome is impossible in an $\mathcal F$-free graph, the few-$H-v$ outcome activates virality inside the $y|G|$-sized subset, and the sparse-pair outcome is already the first alternative.

items.title: Iterated sparse restriction reaches the target sparsity threshold
items.strategy: Starting from the given $c$-sparse induced subgraph, define a sequence of sparsity parameters by repeatedly raising to the power $b_1$. Each application of the hypothesis multiplies the size exponent by at most $b_3$, and the inequality $b_1b_2\ge b_2+b_3$ preserves the lower bound needed to continue the iteration. Stop after the first step that drops below $x$ and compare the resulting size bound with $x^{b_1b_2}|G|$.

items.title: A sparse graph either sparsifies further or yields a comb or a large sparse pair
items.strategy: Assume the graph is not already $2y^4$-sparse and does not already satisfy the large sparse-pair outcome. The new nearly-covered sparse-pair lemma then gives disjoint $A,B$ with $A$ sparse to $B$ and every vertex of $B$ meeting $A$ densely. Use the hitting-set lemma to find a small set $S\subseteq A$ meeting at least half of the neighbourhoods from $B$, and feed the resulting bipartite graph into the published comb theorem. The original high-degree vertex is complete to the comb blocks and anticomplete to the apexes, giving the required third outcome.

title: Iterative Restriction and Comb-Extraction Lemmas — Examples

items.title: The five-vertex path is leaf-reducible
items.strategy: Delete an endpoint of $P_5$ to obtain $P_4$. The published square-root bound for $P_4$-free graphs supplies the smaller family's Erdős–Hajnal property, so the singleton family $\{P_5\}$ satisfies the new definition.

items.title: A nearly covered sparse pair at small parameters
items.strategy: Choose a sparse graph with one high-degree witness vertex, a large set $A$ of its non-neighbours, and a large set $B$ of neighbours each seeing many vertices of $A$. Reading off the inequalities with concrete values of $x$ and $y$ makes the statement of the nearly-covered sparse-pair lemma transparent.

items.title: A numeric run of the multiplicative iteration in Lemma 2.9
items.strategy: Pick explicit parameters $b_1,b_2,b_3,c,x$ satisfying $b_1b_2\ge b_2+b_3$, write down the sequence $c,c^{b_1},c^{b_1^2},\ldots$, and track the size lower bound through two or three steps. The example shows exactly where the exponent inequality is spent.

items.title: A four-tooth comb with an external complete vertex
items.strategy: Write down four apex vertices, four disjoint tooth blocks, and one outside vertex complete to the tooth union and anticomplete to all apexes. This is the finite adjacency pattern that the comb-extraction lemma isolates before any later purity or quotient argument is applied.
